nameStory: The Short-billed Gull gets its straightforward name from its notably compact, stubby bill compared to other gulls of similar size. This bird was previously called the "Mew Gull" in North America because of its distinctive cat-like mewing call that echoes across coastal waters.
description: The Short-billed Gull is a medium-sized gull with clean white plumage, pale gray wings, and yellow legs that make it look quite elegant in flight. Adults are smaller and more delicate-looking than the familiar Herring Gulls you see at beaches, with a rounder head and gentler expression. These gulls typically measure about 16-18 inches long with a wingspan around 3-4 feet. They're most notable for their proportionally short, thin yellow bill that gives them their name.

idTips.label: Bill shape and size
idTips.description: Look for a noticeably short, thin yellow bill that appears almost petite compared to other medium-sized gulls - it's proportionally much smaller than a Ring-billed Gull's bill

idTips.label: Head shape
idTips.description: The head appears rounder and more dove-like than other gulls, giving the bird a gentle, almost innocent expression rather than the fierce look of larger gulls

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: In flight, look for pale gray wings with clean white wing tips that lack the bold black markings seen on Ring-billed or Herring Gulls

idTips.label: Overall size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more compact than Herring Gulls but larger than a crow, with a more delicate build that's apparent even at a distance

idTips.label: Call
idTips.description: Listen for high-pitched mewing calls that sound remarkably cat-like, quite different from the harsh laughing calls of Herring Gulls

habitat: In New England, Short-billed Gulls are most often spotted along rocky coastlines, harbors, and mudflats during migration periods. They prefer quieter coastal areas away from busy beaches, often mixing with flocks of other gulls at fish processing plants or near tidal pools. Look for them around estuaries and salt marshes where they can find small fish and marine invertebrates.

seasonality.spring: Migrating birds may appear along the coast in late spring, often in small numbers mixed with other gull species returning north to their breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in summer as most birds are on their northwestern breeding grounds, though occasional non-breeding individuals might linger along the coast.
seasonality.fall: Peak viewing time as birds migrate south, with juveniles showing brownish mottled plumage that gradually becomes cleaner through the season.
seasonality.winter: Small numbers may overwinter along the New England coast, appearing cleaner and whiter in their adult plumage during this season.

funFact: This gull was only recently recognized as its own species in North America in 2021 - for decades, scientists thought it was the same species as the Common Gull found in Europe and Asia, until genetic studies revealed they're actually distinct species that separated thousands of years ago!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Ring-billed Gulls, but Short-billed Gulls lack the distinctive black ring around the bill and have a much more petite, pointed bill overall. Remember: if you can clearly see a black ring on the bill, it's definitely a Ring-billed Gull, not a Short-billed.
contextualKnowledge: Until very recently, this bird was called the "Mew Gull" in North America and was considered the same species as Europe's Common Gull. The name change and species split happened in 2021, so older field guides and birding resources may still refer to it by its former name, which can be confusing for new birders.
compareHints: Compared to the common Ring-billed Gull, Short-billed Gulls are smaller with cleaner wing tips and lack any dark markings on the bill. They're much smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with proportionally shorter bills and rounder heads. The Short-billed Gull's gentle expression and petite bill make it look almost dove-like compared to its more robust gull relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's large gulls, American Herring Gulls are the 'Goldilocks' species - not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls, not as small as Ring-billed Gulls, but just right in the middle.
Ring-billed Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, lacking the Herring Gull's robust build and pink legs.

Among New England gulls, Great Black-backed Gulls dwarf the common Herring Gull in size and have much darker backs, while Ring-billed Gulls are significantly smaller with lighter grey backs and distinctive black rings around their bills.
Among New England's large gulls, Iceland Gulls are unique for their combination of medium size and extremely pale wing tips.
Among the large white-headed gulls, Lesser Black-backed Gulls are distinguished by their uniquely dark backs - darker than Herring Gulls but not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls.
Among New England's large gulls, Glaucous Gulls stand out for their pale wingtips—Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls both have bold black wingtips, while Ring-billed Gulls are much smaller.
Common Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with yellow-green (not orange-red) bills and legs, plus a gentler facial expression.
Compared to the common Herring Gull, the Slaty-backed Gull has a noticeably darker slate-gray back and is generally larger and more robust.
Unlike Ring-billed Gulls which have a black ring on a yellow bill, Black-tailed Gulls have a red spot and often a black band near the bill tip.
Among the large white-headed gulls in its genus, the California Gull is most similar to the Ring-billed and Herring Gulls but sits between them in size.
Unlike the common white-bodied gulls of New England like Herring and Ring-billed Gulls, Heermann's Gull has the reverse color scheme with a dark body and white head.
